title: My family
goal: Name family members, show ownership with mon/ma/mes, and give your age with avoir — not être.
bekal: name close and extended family members
use possessives that agree with the thing owned, not the owner
give your age: *j'ai vingt ans*, not *je suis vingt ans*
wave: Go back to **Unit 3** first: name ten things around you with their *le* or *la*, then make them all plural.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Les photos de famille
dialogs.intro: Camille shows family photos on her phone.

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Regarde, c'est ma famille. Voici mes parents.
lines.id: Look, this is my family. These are my parents.
lines.literal: look, it-is my(fem.) family. here-are my(pl.) parents.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ton père a l'air jeune ! Il a quel âge ?
lines.id: Your dad looks young! How old is he?
lines.literal: your father has the-air young! he has which age?

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Il a cinquante-huit ans. Et ma mère a cinquante-cinq ans.
lines.id: He's fifty-eight. And my mom is fifty-five.
lines.literal: he has fifty-eight years. and my mother has fifty-five years.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tu as des frères et sœurs ?
lines.id: Do you have any brothers and sisters?
lines.literal: you have some brothers and sisters?

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: J'ai un frère et une sœur. Mon frère est plus âgé.
lines.id: I have one brother and one sister. My brother is older.
lines.literal: I-have a brother and a sister. my brother is more aged.

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Non, ma sœur est mariée. Elle a deux enfants.
lines.id: No, my sister is married. She has two kids.
lines.literal: no, my sister is married. she has two children.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Donc tu es tante ! Et toi, tu as quel âge ?
lines.id: So you're an aunt! And how old are you?
lines.literal: so you are aunt! and you, you have which age?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: J'ai vingt et un ans. Je suis le plus jeune de ma famille.
lines.id: I'm twenty-one. I'm the youngest in my family.
lines.literal: I-have twenty and one years. I am the most young of my family.

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.id: Do your parents live in Jakarta?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Oui, avec ma grand-mère. Elle a quatre-vingt-deux ans.
lines.id: Yes, with my grandmother. She's eighty-two.
lines.literal: yes, with my grandmother. she has four-twenty-two years.

notes: **Age uses avoir, not être.** *J'ai vingt ans* is literally "I have twenty years". Translating straight from English — *je suis vingt ans* — is one of the most common learner mistakes, and to a French ear it sounds like "I am twenty years".
**The word ans can't be dropped.** *J'ai vingt* on its own means nothing. Compare English, where you can just answer "twenty".

**Mon frère, ma sœur, mes parents.** The form agrees with **the thing owned**, not the owner. *Son père* can mean "his father" or "her father" — context tells you which. This is the complete opposite of English *his* vs *her*.
**Avoir l'air** = to look, to seem. *Il a l'air jeune* — literally "he has the air young". The adjective agrees with the person: *elle a l'air fatiguée*.
**Il a quel âge ?** is the most casual form. The full form is *quel âge a-t-il ?*, and the middle one is *quel âge est-ce qu'il a ?* All three are correct; the first is what you'll hear most.
**Vingt et un**, not *vingt-un*. The numbers 21, 31, 41, 51 and 61 slip in an *et*. From 71 on the rule changes again — see Unit 9.
**Quatre-vingt-deux** is literally "four-twenty-two", that is 4×20+2 = 82. Above 60, French numbers really do count in twenties. Don't panic yet; Unit 9 takes it apart slowly.

grammars.title: Avoir — the verb "to have"
body: The second verb you need to know by heart. Besides "to have", it's used for age, hunger, feeling cold, and — later, in Unit 19 — for almost every sentence in the past.
after: ⚠️ *Ils sont* (they are) is said eel SOHN; *ils ont* (they have) is said eel-**Z**OHN. That z sound is the only difference, and beginners always mix them up. Practice the pair out loud until your ear separates them on its own.

Everyday expressions that all use *avoir*: *avoir faim* (to be hungry), *avoir soif* (to be thirsty), *avoir froid* (to be cold), *avoir chaud* (to be hot), *avoir sommeil* (to be sleepy), *avoir peur* (to be afraid), *avoir raison* (to be right), *avoir besoin de* (to need).
All without an article: *j'ai faim*, not *j'ai la faim*.

grammars.title: Possessives
body: Eighteen forms that look like a lot, but are really just six owners times three kinds of thing owned.
after: ⚠️ Before a feminine word starting with a **vowel or silent h**, *ma / ta / sa* become *mon / ton / son* — purely for the sound. Hence *mon amie* (my female friend), *mon école*, *son histoire*. The word doesn't become masculine.
*Notre* and *votre* don't mark gender at all; their plurals are *nos* and *vos*.
*Leur* (one thing owned by several people) versus *leurs* (several things owned by several people): *leur maison* = their house (one house), *leurs enfants* = their children.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *La fille* has two meanings: "daughter" and "girl". Only context and the possessive tell them apart — *ma fille* is definitely my daughter, while *une fille* is a girl.

blocks.title: Family status
items: *Je suis fils unique / fille unique* — I'm an only child.
*l'aîné(e)* — the eldest. *le cadet / la cadette* — the younger one. *le benjamin / la benjamine* — the youngest.
Like English, French has no separate everyday words for older and younger siblings. When it matters: *mon frère aîné* (my big brother), *ma petite sœur* (my little sister).
